--- title: "Hierarchical Bayesian Models" subtitle: "Partial Pooling, Shrinkage, and Group-Level Inference" author: "Suyog Chandramouli" categories: [Bayes] date: '2026-04-13' institute: 'PSY504, Advanced Statistics in Psychology
Princeton University' footer: "PSY 504: Advanced Statistics" format: revealjs: theme: solarized css: slide-style.css transition: fade multiplex: false slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true fontsize: "25pt" execute: freeze: auto eval: true echo: true message: false warning: false fig-align: center fig-width: 12 fig-height: 8 code-overflow: wrap editor: markdown: wrap: sentence --- ::: {.cell} ::: # The Case for Bayesian MLM {.center} ## Where we are **You already know two things:** - How to fit mixed models with `lmer()`: random intercepts, random slopes, crossed effects, ICC, model comparison - How to fit Bayesian regression with `brm()`: priors, posteriors, credible intervals, posterior predictive checks, LOO-CV . . . **Today**: what happens when we combine them ## What does `lme4` actually do? `lme4` uses a procedure equivalent to [empirical Bayes]{.vocab}: - Estimate the variance components via ML or REML (REML is the `lmer` default) - Fix those at plug-in estimates as if they were known - Condition on them to get the random effects (BLUPs) . . . The uncertainty in the variance components is **not propagated** to the group-level estimates. ## A frequentist proof that pooling wins In 1956, Charles Stein proved something that surprised the statistics world: - If you're estimating **three or more group means** at once, estimating each one separately is always beatable - An estimator that pulls groups toward each other will have lower prediction error, on average - Pulling groups toward each other is not a Bayesian idea. It has frequentist proofs. . . . `lmer()` already produces these pulled estimates (shrinkage). The Bayesian model does the same pulling, with full uncertainty about *how much* to pull. ## The right tool for the job ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **Simple balanced experiment** Using Bayes to analyze a clean 2x2 ANOVA is like cutting a birthday cake with a chainsaw. It works, but the extra machinery does nothing. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Multilevel models** Fitting hierarchical models without Bayes is like cutting down a tree with a pocketknife. It works, but you end up making compromises you don't have to make. ::: ::::: . . . Bayes vs. freq differences are more striking with MLMs. ## Frequentist vs. Bayesian {.smaller .shrink} | Aspect | Frequentist | Bayesian | |:-----------------------|:-----------------------|:-----------------------| | **Probability philosophy** | Long-run frequency | Degree of belief | | **Parameters** | Fixed unknowns | Random variables | | **Estimation** | Point estimates (MLE) | Full posteriors | | **Uncertainty** | Confidence intervals | Credible intervals | | **Interpretation** | "95% of samples contain true value" | "95% probability parameter in range" | | **Prior Info** | Not formally used | Explicit priors | | **Prediction** | Points with errors | Full distributions | | **Testing** | p-values | Posterior probabilities | | **Comparison** | AIC, BIC | WAIC, LOO-CV, Bayes Factor | | **Computation** | Often analytical | MCMC sampling | | **Workflow** | Residuals, QQ plots | Posterior checks, Rhat | | **Small Samples** | Often poor | Can be robust | | **R Implementation** | lm(), glmer() | brms::brm(), rstan() | | **Speed** | Faster | More intensive | | **Regularization** | Penalties (LASSO) | Natural via priors | # The Pooling Framework {.center} ## Complete pooling - One grand estimate: ignores groups entirely - Pro: simple, uses all data - Con: misses group-level variation ## No pooling - Each group estimated independently from its own data - Pro: captures group uniqueness - Con: limited by each group's sample size; overfits small groups ## Partial pooling - Groups borrow strength from each other - Small groups have more sampling error; borrowing reduces it - The amount of borrowing is learned from the data ## The group-level standard deviation controls pooling The hyperparameter $\sigma$ (group-level SD) determines the amount of pooling: - $\sigma$ close to 0: groups are nearly identical, recover complete pooling - $\sigma$ very large: groups are essentially independent, recover no pooling - $\sigma$ estimated from data, guided by your prior on $\sigma$ . . . **You do not hand-pick the amount of pooling. The model estimates it from the data, guided by your prior on** $\sigma$. ## The duck-rabbit ![](images/duck-rabbit.jpg){fig-align="center" width="35%"} ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **(a) A description of population structure** Groups come from a population. The model describes that population's distribution. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **(b) A regularization machine** Extreme estimates from small groups get pulled toward the population average. ::: ::::: . . . If you model the population, regularization happens. If you want regularization, model the population. ## What is shrinkage? Partial pooling produces [shrinkage]{.vocab}: estimates pulled toward a common value. - Groups with **few observations** shrink more toward the grand mean - Groups with **many observations** retain their individual character - Groups with **extreme raw estimates** get pulled further . . . Adaptive, automatic, and not a tuning choice. # Three Models in `brms` {.center} ## The radon data EPA measurements of radon gas levels in 919 Minnesota homes across 85 counties. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Bayes_Hierarchical_2026_Students_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Radon data: key variables - **Outcome**: `log_radon` (log of radon gas level) - **Predictor**: `floor` (0 = basement, 1 = first floor) - **Grouping**: `county` (85 Minnesota counties) - **County-level**: `log_uranium` (soil uranium content) ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Bayes_Hierarchical_2026_Students_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Model 1: Complete pooling Ignore counties entirely. One regression for all 919 homes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_pool <- brm( log_radon ~ floor, data = mn_radon, file = "fits/fit_pool" ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fixef(fit_pool) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Estimate Est.Error Q2.5 Q97.5 Intercept 1.3625440 0.02884281 1.3072374 1.4198890 floor -0.5873097 0.06960242 -0.7211983 -0.4532058 ``` ::: ::: ## Model 2: No pooling Each county gets its own intercept, estimated from its own data. (The `floor` slope and residual variance are still shared.) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_nopool <- brm( log_radon ~ 0 + floor + county_id, data = mn_radon, file = "fits/fit_nopool" ) ``` ::: ## Model 3: Partial pooling Counties share a common distribution. Each county's estimate borrows strength from the others. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit_partial <- brm( log_radon ~ floor + (1 | county_id), prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept) + prior(exponential(1), class = sd) + prior(exponential(1), class = sigma), data = mn_radon, file = "fits/fit_partial" ) ``` ::: The formula is the same as `lmer()`: `(1 | county_id)` The one addition: `prior(exponential(1), class = sd)` ## Visualizing shrinkage ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayesplot::mcmc_intervals(fit_partial, regex_pars = "r_county") + bayesplot::yaxis_text(FALSE) + labs(title = "County-level intercept deviations (partial pooling)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Bayes_Hierarchical_2026_Students_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## The partial pooling summary ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(fit_partial) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Family: gaussian Links: mu = identity Formula: log_radon ~ floor + (1 | county_id) Data: mn_radon (Number of observations: 919) Draws: 4 chains, each with iter = 2000; warmup = 1000; thin = 1; total post-warmup draws = 4000 Multilevel Hyperparameters: ~county_id (Number of levels: 85) Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS sd(Intercept) 0.32 0.04 0.24 0.41 1.00 1518 2312 Regression Coefficients: Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS Intercept 1.49 0.05 1.39 1.59 1.00 2617 2867 floor -0.66 0.07 -0.80 -0.53 1.00 8123 3054 Further Distributional Parameters: Estimate Est.Error l-95% CI u-95% CI Rhat Bulk_ESS Tail_ESS sigma 0.73 0.02 0.69 0.76 1.00 6334 3144 Draws were sampled using sampling(NUTS). For each parameter, Bulk_ESS and Tail_ESS are effective sample size measures, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence, Rhat = 1). ``` ::: ::: # Syntax (lme4 vs. brms) {.center} ## `lmer()` and `brm()`: same formula | | Formula | |:-------------|:--------------------------------------------------| | `lmer()` | `mean_pupil ~ vocoded + (1 + vocoded \| subject)` | | `brm()` | `mean_pupil ~ vocoded + (1 + vocoded \| subject)` | | What changes | Add `prior(exponential(1), class = sd)` | . . . The formula syntax is **identical**. The difference is that `brms` puts an explicit prior on $\sigma$ (the group-level SD), while `lme4` fixes it at a plug-in estimate. ## `ranef()` vs. `coef()` in `brms` ::: {.cell} ::: Two ways to summarize group-level parameters: - `ranef()` (**ran**dom **ef**fects, or "group-level effects" in `brms`) returns **deviations** around the grand mean ($u_{0i}$) - `coef()` (**coef**ficients, or "population-level + group-level" in `brms`) returns the **actual group intercepts** ($\beta_0 + u_{0i}$) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Deviations from grand mean ranef(fit_partial) # Actual county-level intercepts coef(fit_partial) ``` ::: ## Bayes advantage: group-level credible intervals ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coef(fit_partial)$county_id[, , "Intercept"] %>% data.frame() %>% arrange(Estimate) %>% mutate(rank = 1:n()) %>% bind_rows( fixef(fit_partial) %>% data.frame() %>% filter(row.names(.) == "Intercept") %>% mutate(rank = 0) ) %>% mutate(type = ifelse(rank == 0, "Grand mean", "County intercept")) %>% ggplot(aes(x = Estimate, xmin = Q2.5, xmax = Q97.5, y = rank, color = type)) + geom_pointrange(size = 1/3) + scale_color_manual(NULL, values = c("Grand mean" = "red", "County intercept" = "steelblue")) + scale_y_continuous("Rank order", breaks = c(1, 25, 50, 75)) + xlab("Log radon level") + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Bayes_Hierarchical_2026_Students_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## The group-level variance parameter ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as_draws_df(fit_partial) %>% ggplot(aes(x = sd_county_id__Intercept)) + stat_halfeye(.width = .95, fill = "steelblue") + scale_x_continuous(expression(sigma[county]), limits = c(0, NA)) + scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL) + theme_bw(base_size = 18) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Bayes_Hierarchical_2026_Students_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: $\sigma_{county} \approx 0.3$ — the population SD of county-level radon intercepts. # Testing and Practical Workflow {.center} ## HDI-based significance Does the 95% credible interval for a fixed effect exclude zero? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} posteriors <- as_draws_df(fit_partial) hdi(posteriors$b_floor, ci = 0.95) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 95% HDI: [-0.79, -0.53] ``` ::: ::: . . . If the HDI excludes zero, the effect is credibly different from zero at 95%. ## Posterior predictive check ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pp_check(fit_partial, ndraws = 100) + theme_bw(base_size = 18) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Bayes_Hierarchical_2026_Students_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ## Building hierarchical models incrementally McElreath's practical workflow: 1. Start with **intercepts-only**: `y ~ 1 + (1 | group)` 2. Run **prior predictive checks** on the hierarchical structure 3. Fit and check **diagnostics** (ESS, Rhat, especially for $\sigma$) 4. If you see **divergences**, increase `adapt_delta` (e.g., `control = list(adapt_delta = 0.95)`) 5. **Prior-posterior overlap** for $\sigma$ is common and expected — data often cannot fully learn the variance structure 6. Add **varying slopes** if theoretically motivated ## Watch for these diagnostics | Diagnostic | What it tells you | Worry threshold | |:------------|:-------------------------|:----------------| | Rhat | Chain convergence | Above 1.01 | | Bulk ESS | Posterior body sampling | Below 400 | | Tail ESS | Posterior tail sampling | Below 400 | | Divergences | Funnel geometry problems | Any above 0 | Divergences in hierarchical models often mean the sampler is struggling with the "funnel" shape of the posterior where $\sigma$ is small. # Lab Preview {.center} ## What you'll do in the lab 1. Load a grouped dataset 2. Fit a **complete pooling** model (no group structure) 3. Fit a **no pooling** model (fixed effects for each group) 4. Fit a **partial pooling** model (random intercepts) 5. Compare shrinkage: which groups move most? 6. Visualize group-level credible intervals 7. Run posterior predictive checks 8. Compare models with **LOO-CV** (`loo_compare()`) ## Resources - Gelman & Hill (2007). *Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models* - McElreath (2020). *Statistical Rethinking*, Chapters 12--13 - Kurz (2023). *Introduction to Bayesian Statistics with brms and the tidyverse* (Module 19) # Optional: Bayes Factors for Parameter Testing {.center} ## Testing parameters with Bayes Factors Can we test whether a specific effect is zero? - Use `bayesfactor_parameters()` from `bayestestR` - Requires `sample_prior = "yes"` and an explicit prior ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Fit with prior sampling enabled fit_bf <- brm( log_radon ~ floor + (1 | county_id), prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = Intercept) + prior(normal(0, 1), class = b) + prior(exponential(1), class = sd) + prior(exponential(1), class = sigma), data = mn_radon, sample_prior = "yes", file = "fits/fit_bf" ) # Test floor effect against zero bayesfactor_parameters(fit_bf, null = 0) ``` ::: ## Comparing full models with Bayes Factors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Compare models with different fixed effects fit_bf1 <- brm( log_radon ~ floor + (1 | county_id), prior = prior(normal(0, 1), class = b) + prior(exponential(1), class = sd), data = mn_radon, sample_prior = "yes", save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE), file = "fits/fit_bf1" ) fit_bf2 <- brm( log_radon ~ 1 + (1 | county_id), prior = prior(exponential(1), class = sd), data = mn_radon, sample_prior = "yes", save_pars = save_pars(all = TRUE), file = "fits/fit_bf2" ) bayesfactor_models(fit_bf1, fit_bf2) ``` ::: ## Tomorrow: Tracy Sweet **Tracy Sweet** -- Associate Professor, University of Maryland QMMS Psychometric Computation and Simulation (PCS) Lab **Network Science in Psychology** - Apr 14, 2026, 12:00 pm -- 1:00 pm - A30, Princeton Neuroscience Institute

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
